title: He Called Out Thomas Jefferson. In Writing.

beats.text: He called out Thomas Jefferson. In writing.

overlays.hook: He called out Thomas Jefferson. *In writing.*

beats.text: Born free in Maryland in 1731, he had almost no schooling.
At about twenty-two, he built a striking clock almost entirely out of wood. It reportedly ran for decades.
Later, with borrowed books, he taught himself astronomy, and predicted a solar eclipse.
In 1791, he helped survey the land for the new capital, the future Washington, D.C.
That year, he wrote to Thomas Jefferson, who wrote that all men are created equal, and held people in slavery.

visual.caption: Copy of a Letter from Benjamin Banneker to the Secretary of State, 1792

beats.text: Banneker quoted his own words back to him, and accused him of holding people by fraud and violence.
He enclosed his own almanac, as proof of what a Black man could do.
Jefferson wrote back, and sent the almanac to the Academy of Sciences in Paris.
Banneker died in 1806. On the day of his funeral, his house burned, and his clock with it.
He called out Thomas Jefferson. In writing.

facts.claim: Born 9 Nov 1731, Baltimore County, Maryland, to a free mother; little schooling.
About age 22, built a striking clock almost entirely of wood from his own drawings; reportedly ran ~40 years.
From 1788, with books/instruments lent by George Ellicott, taught himself astronomy and calculated a solar eclipse.
1791: worked with Andrew Ellicott on the survey of the federal district (about two months).
Letter to Jefferson, 19 Aug 1791, quoting 'all men are created equal' against slavery.
The letter says Jefferson was 'detaining by fraud and violence' people in bondage.
Jefferson replied 30 Aug 1791 and sent the almanac to Condorcet, Secretary of the Academy of Sciences in Paris.
Died 1806; his house and its contents, including the clock, burned on the day of his funeral.

notUsed: That he laid out Washington D.C. or redrew L'Enfant's plan from memory: a myth
'America's first clock' or 'first striking clock': unproven
Exact death date (9 or 19 Oct 1806, sources differ)
Wikipedia says the clock worked until his death but doesn't mention the fire destroying it; PBS says the fire destroyed it
